analytic.title: Real-time Scheduling Of Sporadic Tasks In Energy Harvesting Distributed Reconfigurable Embedded Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper explores the energy-aware strategy for adaptive task allocation of sporadic task model in distributed reconfigurable embedded systems powered by a renewable energy source. It is challenging to ensure hard real-time deadlines of sporadic tasks in distributed reconfigurable embedded systems that entirely rely on energy harvesting with limited capacity storage because their release times and periods are unknown beforehand. In this regard, we propose a new scheduling algorithm for sporadic task model in energy harvesting reconfigurable distributed embedded system. The proposed approach generates an energy efficient offline task assignment heuristic. Then, the offline stage is dynamically extended online by applying a dynamic adaption algorithm. The latter performs three solutions: i) Migration, ii) Degradation of the execution mode, and iii) Removal of tasks in order to maintain schedulability and sustainability of the application software. Simulations show the efficiency of the proposed approach in term of deadline success ratio.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Distributed embedded systems are increasingly deployed in various applications ranging from our daily lives to industry production, in avionic, automobile, telecommunications, the control aircraft, medical equipment, nuclear and chemical plants, and power distribution systems. Most of these applications are real-time constrained. The correctness of these architectures depends not only upon their accurate results, but also upon the imposed deadlines in which the results are delivered [1]. The real-time systems are classified by the consequences of missing a deadline as: (i) Hard real-time systems where the non respect of timing requirements may lead to severe consequences, and (ii) Soft real-time systems where missing some deadlines may be tolerable [2]- [4].

Further, many of these embedded systems are batterypowered. Obviously, these batteries have limited energy storage capacity and therefore, finite useful life. However, replacing batteries in due time is either impractical or prohibitively expensive. The energy harvesting technology emerges as a promising alternative to enhance the system's lifetime and to achieve energy autonomy. Several technologies are proposed for harvesting energy from environmental sources, include solar cells, water or wind flow, piezoelectric vibration, and thermal and acoustic noise. In particular, solar energy harvesting provides relatively higher power densities which makes it increasingly deployed to design energy harvesting embedded systems. In an energy harvesting-based system, the main issue is to guarantee that at any moment the system does not consume more energy than harvested and available in the storage. However, realizing such systems that meet energy requirements and application's performance is nontrivial due to many factors and a number of challenges arise. The uncertainty in the energy availability provided by free sources makes the developing of reliable and energy-efficient power-management solutions more challenging.

There is an increasing trend to develop reconfigurable computing systems due to their potential to greatly satisfy the simultaneous demand for application performance and flexibility [5], [6], [7]. Some academic and industrial research works have been made in recent years to develop reconfigurable control systems [8], [9]. A reconfigurable computing system undergoes unpredictable events that require adequate online decisions so as to maintain schedulability of the application software. Thereafter, some existing or added tasks may violate deadlines due to energy starvation or processing overload, for example. Therefore, energy autonomy in networked reconfigurable embedded systems is a major concern. To tackle this problem, an efficient solution is to use energy management policies that dynamically schedule the available energy according to real-time system states. Although there are a large number of studies focusing on harvested-energy management that adapt the system to uncertainty in energy availability by deploying energy harvesting prediction algorithm [10], [11], most existing studies do not consider dynamic reconfiguration scenarios that may lead to deadline violation and/or energy starvation. Moreover, most of these approaches are proposed for periodic and aperiodic task models, yet there are few algorithms that support the sporadic task model. Sporadic tasks are a kind of tasks that recur at random instants and represent an important part in real-time system applications. It is challenging to schedule sporadic tasks because neither the time of occurrence, nor the reoccurrence of such tasks is known beforehand.

Therefore, one focus of this paper is to study this more difficult problem of scheduling energy harvesting reconfigurable real-time embedded system modeled as collection of sporadic tasks, upon a distributed architecture. We consider a distributed reconfigurable embedded energy harvesting system composed of multiple networked subsystems. Each subsystem is composed of one processor and one rechargeable energy storage unit with limited capacity supplied by a renewable energy source. We assume that the system is composed of a set of heterogeneous processors where preemption and migration of tasks are authorized. Moreover, we assume that the cost of migration is subsumed into the worst-case execution time of each task. The system handles two sets of independent sporadic tasks: i) Critical tasks set, and ii) Non-critical tasks set. A sporadic task τ i is characterized by its relative deadline minimum inter-arrival time and worst-case execution time. We assume that the system can be reconfigured repeatedly. Thereafter, some existing or added tasks may violate deadlines due to energy starvation or processing overload, for example. Therefore, the main issue is to guarantee that all critical tasks will meet their deadlines. Additionally, we aim to minimize the miss deadline ratio of non-critical tasks. The major contributions of this paper are:

• A novel sporadic task allocation algorithm for energy harvesting distributed embedded system that operates in two stages. A static stage executed offline in order to guarantee the feasibility of the critical sporadic tasks set by considering the worst case scenario. The offline stage is dynamically extended online by applying a dynamic adaption algorithm. The online stage aim to reuse the slack resources such as energy and processor load to schedule the non critical tasks. • A dynamic adjustment stage performs three solutions: i) Migration, ii) Degradation of the execution mode, and iii) Removal of tasks in order to maintain schedulability and sustainability of the application software whenever a reconfiguration scenario applied at run-time wants to add a critical task. • The performance of the proposed approach is evaluated in term of deadline success ratio.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work on energy harvesting aware sporadic task allocation to reconfigurable distributed embedded systems. The paper is organized as follows. Section II gives a brief state of the art about sporadic task scheduling, energy aware scheduling, and reconfigurable real-time systems. Section III formalizes the system model and section IV describes our proposed approach for real-time scheduling with energy harvesting predictions. Section V describes the proposed approach for sporadic task scheduling in the presence of reconfiguration scenarios applied repeatedly at run-time. Section VI reports simulation results that bring to light the effectiveness of these solutions measured in term of deadline success ratio. Finally we conclude in Section VII with a summary of our contributions.

div.head: II. RELATED WORKS
div.p: In this section, we present a state of the art dealing first with sporadic task scheduling, then real-time scheduling under energy harvesting constraints, and finally distributed reconfigurable embedded systems.

div.head: A. Sporadic Task Scheduling
div.p: Over the years, the literature has revealed an immense research attention to the sporadic task model, which presents an extension of the earlier task model of Liu and Layland (LL) [12]. In the real-time community, a number of research works have proposed to treat the sporadic tasks as periodic tasks where the minimum inter-arrival time is considered as an exact period. In [13], the authors consider sporadic tasks with minimum inter-arrival time as periodic tasks for the preemptive scheduling of hard real-time sporadic task systems on uniprocessor. The authors propose an exact schedulability analysis where they provide some necessary and sufficient conditions for a sporadic task system to be schedulable. The authors of [14] have proposed a method to transform the sporadic task parameters to create periodic reservation tasks. However, considering sporadic tasks as periodic tasks where the exact period is equal to the minimum inter-arrival times, can overestimate the number of task arrivals and may lead to a pessimistic schedulability analysis. Isovic and Fohler [15], [16], [17] have worked on the combined offline and online approach for efficient scheduling of real-time tasks. In [17], the authors propose a combined offline and online approach to handle event-triggered sporadic tasks with unknown arrival times, but known maximum arrival frequencies. The proposed algorithm is based on the slot shifting method, which provides for the combination of time-triggered offline schedule construction and on-line scheduling of aperiodic activities. At runtime, it uses the slot shifting mechanisms to feasibly schedule sporadic tasks in union with the off-line scheduled periodic tasks, while allowing resources to be reclaimed for aperiodic tasks. Recently, researches on energy conservation of sporadic tasks have been presented. All of these research works do not consider the energy harvesting context.

div.head: B. Real-Time Scheduling with Energy Harvesting Requirements
div.p: More recently, Chetto [18] has proposed energy-aware scheduling algorithm, namely ED-H, based on the EDF rule, proved to be optimal and appropriate for the scheduling of real-time jobs in general. Therefore, there are no restrictions on this new scheduler. Each job can be one instance of a periodic, aperiodic, or sporadic task with deadline. However, the literature has revealed several important works focused on the scheduling in uniprocessor energy harvesting based embedded systems [19], [18], [20], but the energy harvesting aware scheduling for the multiprocessor case has received much less attention. The research work in [21] defines an efficient particular EDF scheduling algorithm called EH-EDF (Energy Harvesting-Earliest Deadline First) for aperiodic tasks, where decisions are taken at run-time without having prior knowledge about the future energy production and task characteristics. The research work in [22] defines an epoch-based approach for the energy management in performance constrained WSNs that utilizes energy harvesting solutions. The proposed approach utilizes two energy management techniques, Dynamic Voltage Scaling (DVS) and Dynamic Modulation Scaling (DMS). The authors of [23] propose an energy-efficient fault tolerance task allocation scheme for multiprocessor SoCs in real-time embedded energy harvesting systems. The proposed task allocation scheme achieves fault tolerance by reserving enough slack on each processing element and by re-executing the faulty task when the fault occurs. Major prior existing works on real-time scheduling in energy harvesting systems addressed periodic task model. They mainly focus on uniprocessor architectures even with DVFS facilities. However, these results cannot be simply extended to sporadic task model in a distributed context and they cannot obtain good performance when scheduling sporadic tasks. Nevertheless, none of these works consider the challenges arising from the uncertainty in the energy availability provided by ambient sources.

div.head: C. Reconfigurable Real-Time Systems
div.p: There is currently a great interest in developing reconfigurable embedded systems from academic and industrial works [24]. The work in [25] proposes a novel approach for the management of safe reconfigurations of agent-based reconfigurable embedded control systems (ECS). The research in [26] proposes a new coordination method for a distributed reconfigurable discrete event control system (DRDECS) where each subsystem is modeled by a reconfigurable timed net condition/event system. The paper develops a virtual coordinator and a communication protocol in order to treat all concurrent reconfiguration requirements using judgement matrices while the exchanged messages are reduced. However, all of these works cope with reconfigurable distributed embedded systems but no one among them deals with energy requirements. Power consumption and energy requirements for the reconfigurable distributed embedded systems have received much less attention. Among the most interesting studies, the research in [27], a software-agent-based architecture provides four solutions to reconfigure the system at run-time. In addition, the agent provides three virtual processors in order to reduce the system's power consumption. However, no work deals with energy harvesting assumptions.

To the best of our knowledge, no work from the state of the art deals with mixed critical sporadic task model scheduling in a reconfigurable distributed embedded system with energy harvesting assumptions. As far as we know, the work reported in this paper is the first one that focuses on scheduling of real-time sporadic tasks in a reconfigurable multiprocessor energy harvesting real-time system based on energy harvesting predictions algorithm.

2) Pre-Energy: Solar Energy Predictor: In this section, we discuss the energy prediction algorithm for distributed reconfigurable embedded systems proposed in our previous work [28]. The later combines historical observations based on learning machines, local observations, and weather forecast in the purpose to derive more efficient and precise predictions on the future energy availability. The literature has revealed several works developed to predict the solar energy using machine learning techniques and environmental parameters. The Gaussian processes regression (GPR) have been proved more robust than other regression appraoches. Therefore, our prediction model has its foundation on GPR [29], [30].

For energy management and prediction, we consider a prediction interval I discretized into N equal duration time slots. In order to predict the harvesting energy incoming in the future for a slot s on an interval I, E e (s, I), the preenergy algorithm combines two terms: i) The historical energy estimation E h (s, I), and ii) The current interval's elapsed slot energy estimation E e (s -1, I).

A storage unit is defined by B j = (E jmax , E jmin ), ∀j = {1, ..., m} where E jmax and E jmin are respectively the minimal and maximal energy that can be stored. The energy available in the storage B j at a particular time t is denoted by E Bj (t). We also assume that each energy storage can be charged up to its capacity.

div.head: C. Task Model
div.p: We assume that the system Sys performs two classes of tasks: i) A critical task set ψ c containing n tasks ψ c = {τ 1 , .., τ n }, and ii) A non-critical task set ψ nc containing m tasks ψ nc = {τ 1 , .., τ m }. Each task τ i is characterized by a three tuple (T i , C i , D i ), where T i is the minimum interval between two executions of task τ i , C i is the worst-case execution time WCET, and D i is the relative deadline. In addition, we characterize a task τ i with a worst case energy consumption (WCEC) En i . Each task is independent and preemptive and has implicit deadlines, i.e., deadlines are equal to periods. The costs of scheduler invocations, preemptions, and migrations are not modeled. In the areas of avionics and automotive, many sporadic tasks such as "Reinitiate Trajectory" are highly critical in nature and meeting the task's deadline is critical to the system's operation, while others such "Change Display" are soft real-time task and it is desirable to meet the task's deadline but occasionally missing the deadline can be tolerated. Hence, the embedded real-time system is known as a mixed-criticality system. Such that, we characterize sporadic tasks with a degree of criticality dc i that defines its applicative importance. A critical task τ i is characterized by: (T i , D i , C i , En i , dc i ). Moreover, a non critical task τ i is characterized by a (m i , k i ) parameter which indicates that we tolerate that at least m instances among k consecutive ones must respect their deadlines for the task τ i . div.head: IV. SPORADIC TASK SCHEDULING WITH ENERGY HARVESTING PREDICTION
div.p: Sporadic task scheduling on a reconfigurable distributed embedded system is a NP-complete problem. This paper addresses the even more difficult problem of scheduling on systems constrained by both real-time constraint and energy constraint due to the uncertainty of the energy availability profile. To address these challenges, we propose a workload semi-dynamic management framework based on the energy harvesting availability predictions. The major objective of our algorithm is to guarantee that all critical tasks will succeed their deadlines over the system's execution time. Additionally, we aim to minimize the miss deadline ratio of the non critical tasks.

div.head: A. Motivation
div.p: We assume that all sporadic tasks will be invoked with their maximum frequency, creating the worst case scenario for the scheduler. However, a sporadic task which is released with its maximum frequency behaves exactly like a periodic task with a period equals to its minimum inter-arrival time, which may lead the schedulability analysis to be pessimistic and overestimates the number of task arrivals. Therefore, we propose a new two stages algorithm which adopts a dynamic adjustment phase to reduce pessimism about possible future arrivals to guarantee the feasibility of the critical tasks set. This set is guaranteed offline before the run-time of the system. Therefore, an offline test determines and allocates resources for sporadic critical tasks such that worst case arrivals can be considered. Nevertheless, a large amount of slack time and energy exists due to the difference between the actual arrival pattern time of the sporadic critical task and the worst case sequence of arrivals as depicted in Fig. 1. However, at runtime, when a critical sporadic task does not arrive we can reuse its allocated resources for a non critical sporadic task.
In the following sections, we describe in detail the proposed approach.

div.head: B. Offline Phase: Semi-partitioned Task Assignment Heuristic
div.p: The static task allocation problem is divided into two steps. The first one is the assigning of the critical tasks set. The main objective for the first step is to guarantee that all the critical tasks will met their hard deadlines. The second step aims to assign the non-critical tasks. The objective of the second step is to reduce the miss deadline ratio of the non critical-tasks set. The following steps describe the basic idea of our proposed energy harvesting task allocation heuristic:

Step 1: Sort the set of critical tasks in a decreasing order of degree of criticity dc i , Step 2: Assign task τ i to processor P j where the real-time and energy constraints are satisfied, Step 3: Assign the set of non-critical tasks to the set of processors if possible. The offline phase: semi-partitioned task assignment heuristic algorithm is described in Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2.

div.head: V. SPORADIC TASK SCHEDULING IN THE PRESENCE OF RECONFIGURATION SCENARIOS
A. Motivation
div.p: A run-time external reconfiguration scenario is assumed to be any dynamic operation allowing the addition/removal of critical and non-critical tasks. Thereafter, some tasks may miss their hard deadlines and the energy constraint may be violated. Therefore, the system feasibility should be validated after any reconfiguration scenarios. Further, each processor in the multiprocessor platform should satisfy the hard realtime constraint in which the CPU processor utilization is no greater than the schedulable utilization U x , in addition to the energy constraint where the processor's energy consumption is at most equal to the energy harvested in the storage associated to the processor. If the system feasibility is satisfied then the system operates normally. Besides, if at least one of the feasibility conditions is violated then the dynamic software reconfiguration solutions are applied one by one in order to reconfigure the system and re-establish the system feasibility. Therefore, the dynamic adaption phase is performed whenever a dynamic reconfiguration scenario applied at run-time makes the system evolving towards an infeasible state. The dynamic adaption algorithm performs three solutions: i) Migration, iii) Degradation of the execution mode of the non-critical tasks and ii) Removal of non-critical tasks. The three solutions are performed in a hierarchical order:

• Migrate critical or non-critical tasks from one processor to another one, • Degrade the quality of service. Non-critical tasks may be executed according to (m,k)-firm constraints, • Delete non-critical tasks so as to minimize the global deadline miss ratio. 1) Migration Solution: This solution proposes to migrate a task from a faulty processor to a non faulty one. Hence, the solution is performed in two steps: the first step selects the task or the tasks to be migrated. The second step selects the processor where the tasks will be affected.

div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: We explore in this section the performance of the proposed algorithms in the presence of the variable solar based energy harvesting. In order to evaluate this approach, we consider a set of 50 sporadic tasks generated with utilization factors evenly distributed within [umin, umax] = [0.1, 1.00], to be schedulable on three heterogeneous processors platform. The minimum inter-arrival time T i of each task is chosen randomly in the range of [10,100]. Task WCETs C i are computed from periods T i and utilization factors U i : C i = T i *U i . We assume a set of unpredictable reconfiguration scenarios applied repeatedly. Each scenario adds a set of n tasks such that n is randomly chosen between 50 and 100. For the harvested energy we assume that the interval time I is equal to a day, data is collected through PVP SM50-H (Siemens) [33]. Battery charge (A-h) is measured at the end of every slot that reflects the harvested energy within that slot. The data is collected after every one hour slot. First slot starts from 5.30 AM in the morning and finishes at 7.00PM that present sunrise and sunset in the area of Tunisia in the month of April. We have run several sets of simulations to investigate the performance of:

i) The task assignment algorithm, ii) The dynamic adaption algorithm, iii) The proposed approach in the presence of unpredictable reconfiguration scenarios. The performance evaluation of the proposed task assignment algorithm and dynamic adaption algorithm in terms of our objectives which are minimizing the miss ratio deadline of non-critical tasks and to guarantee that all critical tasks will meet their hard deadlines. Fig. 2 presents the success ratio for both critical and non-critical tasks set by implementing the combined approach offline and online stages. It can be derived from this figure that the success ratio for the non critical tasks set achieves 78.64% when the system utilization is equal to three. Moreover, Fig. 2 shows clearly that the proposed approach succeed to schedule the set of critical tasks where the success ratio is equal to 90.04% when utilization factor is equal to three. We evaluate the performance of the proposed approach when a set of unpredictable reconfiguration scenarios are applied repeatedly at run-time. We assume that a set of four reconfiguration scenarios occur at run-time where each one adds 50 sporadic tasks. Fig. 3 presents the percentage of satisfied deadlines for the migration, degradation and removal tasks solutions. It clearly shows that the performance of all algorithms degrades when the number of tasks increases due to a set of reconfiguration scenarios applied repeatedly at run-time. However, the proposed approach permits to succeed 71.96% of the critical tasks set and 52.89% of the non critical tasks set, when the number of tasks is equal to 250 tasks.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we presented a two stages algorithm for sporadic task scheduling problem in reconfigurable real-time distributed embedded systems powered by energy harvesting. The offline phase aims to guarantee the critical task set by considering the worst case arrivals times for critical sporadic tasks. However, considering sporadic tasks as periodic tasks where the exact period is equal to the minimum inter-arrival times, can overestimate the number of task arrivals and may lead to a pessimistic schedulability analysis. Therefore, a dynamic adjustment phase executed online is proposed in order to reuse the non used allocated resources in the aim to schedule the non critical tasks set. Furthermore, we proposed a dynamic adaption algorithm which performs three solutions: i) Migration, ii) Degradation of the execution mode, and iii) Removal of tasks in order to deal with unpredictable reconfiguration scenarios. To the best of our knowledge, the work reported in this paper is the first one that focuses on scheduling of realtime sporadic tasks in a reconfigurable multiprocessor realtime system based on energy harvesting predictions algorithm. The goals are to guarantee that all critical tasks succeeded their hard deadlines, while minimizing the miss deadline ratio of non critical tasks under energy neutrality consideration. Extensive simulation experiments show that the proposed approach achieves the deadline success ratio up to 90.04% for the set of critical tasks and up to 78.64% for the set of non-critical tasks when the system utilization is equal to three.

We plan in a future work to propose a novel scheduling algorithm for distributed reconfigurable energy harvesting systems based on the sporadic task model where we characterize the arrival times with probabilistic distributions.
